title: General-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a programmable digital processor that performs reliable general computation while dissipating energy close to the thermodynamic scale associated with information erasure. It would recover much of the energy used to switch its circuits and reuse that energy in subsequent operations. The target combines near-room-temperature operation, useful computation and complete system energy accounting; an efficient isolated gate would establish only part of this capability.

Landauer’s principle assigns a minimum mean heat cost of kT ln 2 to ideal erasure of an initially unbiased classical bit in the usual isothermal setting, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is absolute temperature. At 300 K, this is approximately 2.9×10⁻²¹ joule. Logical reversibility means preserving enough information to reconstruct the input from the output, so an operation need not incur this particular erasure cost. It does not automatically make a physical circuit lossless: switching, control, communication and error management can still dissipate energy.

Logical reversibility and adiabatic energy recovery address complementary problems. Reversibility avoids unnecessary destruction of information; adiabatic switching seeks to recover circuit signal energy through controlled physical transitions. The intended processor must combine these principles across programs, including the information that eventually must be erased, rather than treating low-energy switching alone as evidence of low-energy computation.

significance.text: A processor meeting this target at useful throughput and density would establish a major capability in energy-efficient digital computation. Its direct benefit would be lower energy consumption and heat generation per completed computation under the demonstrated operating conditions. The supplied reporting and preliminary conventional-CMOS analysis motivate a substantial gap between present switching energies and thermodynamic information scales, while the retained roadmap text describes limited further improvements from conventional scaling. The supplied evidence does not establish a precise universal CMOS energy range.

Low dissipation per erased bit is insufficient by itself to establish this benefit. A reversible implementation might perform many additional operations or retain and move substantial intermediate information. Memory, communication, correction and control could consume the apparent savings. The decisive comparison is therefore total wall-plug energy per useful workload at specified throughput, reliability and resource use. The preliminary Frank–Edwards analysis explicitly leaves architectural overheads outside some of its efficiency projections.

Conditional impact synthesis: if the savings survived those system costs, the technology could ease power and cooling constraints and expand what energy-limited computers can accomplish. Comparing its potential importance with the transistor expresses the scale of the ambition: a change in the practical cost of a basic computational resource. It does not establish equivalent economic impact, competitive manufacturing costs or widespread adoption. Those outcomes would require additional engineering and commercial evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is to combine information-preserving logic, efficient physical energy recovery and reliable programmable execution in a scalable processor near room temperature. The supplied historical results establish ingredients and proposed approaches, but do not demonstrate this complete combination. They also do not establish whether the complete target remains unmet as of 1 November 2026, because the supplied record contains no subsequent-progress search.

Energy recovered from a switching device must remain useful after losses in the clock, resonator, power delivery and associated control circuitry. A circuit can recover signal energy locally while still drawing substantial external power. The Spectrum account describes this difficulty in earlier reversible-computing prototypes, and Herr’s analysis emphasizes accounting that includes the clock source. Resolving this requires energy recovery to work across the complete physical system, rather than moving dissipation outside the measured device.

Thermal fluctuations, fabrication variation and nonideal switching must be managed without losing the energy advantage. Herr’s superconducting model illustrates how device mismatch can raise dissipation above the ideal value, although its 4.2 K operating conditions do not establish the corresponding behavior near room temperature. A practical design must also balance switching speed against dissipation: approaching an erasure bound through very long cycles does not demonstrate useful processor throughput.

System-level synthesis: programmable operation adds the challenge of managing intermediate information, memory traffic, communication and correction without excessive extra work. Reversible-operation counts and unavoidable information erasure must be defined consistently enough to connect device measurements to workload energy. The missing capability is therefore both physical and architectural: low-loss components must support complete programs whose total energy remains close to the intended scale.

current_state.text: Bérut, Arakelyan, Petrosyan, Ciliberto, Dillenschneider and Lutz reported a single-bit colloidal-memory experiment in Nature 483, 187–189, published 7 March 2012, DOI 10.1038/nature10872. A colloidal particle in a modulated double-well potential represented the bit, and the reported mean dissipated heat approached the Landauer bound for long erasure cycles. This supports the erasure principle in that experimental setting; it is not a demonstration of a programmable reversible processor or an experimental verification of all reversible operations. The supplied review had access to the abstract and publication metadata, rather than the full experimental methods and results.

A Frank–Edwards presentation dated 30 October 2023 discusses projected conventional-CMOS efficiency limits and adiabatic energy recovery. It identifies its analysis as preliminary and notes that architectural overheads of adiabatic and reversible designs have not yet been included in some projections. The retained text supports its technical motivation, but the review did not independently inspect numerical graphical results. Separately, the candidate cites a Frank–Edwards article in APL Electronic Devices 1, 030902, dated 29 September 2025, DOI 10.1063/5.0279617, and attributes a projected signal-energy floor of 25,200 kT to it. No artifact of that article was retained, so its bibliographic details, numerical value and context remain unverified in this record. The 2023 presentation cannot substitute for the missing article.

The retained 2022 IRDS More Moore roadmap text describes limits on further reductions in switching energy from conventional scaling. Its extraction was truncated, and some pages lacked extractable text. Consequently, the supplied review supports the qualitative scaling limitation but does not establish a precise numerical floor from the roadmap’s tables or figures.

IEEE Spectrum’s article of 2 January 2025, updated 22 May 2025, reports Vaire Computing’s announcement of a prototype tape-out and its claimed capability to recover 50% of the energy used in the resonator circuit. Tape-out and a reported company capability claim do not establish independently measured operating performance. The percentage concerns resonator-circuit energy, not total processor energy or Landauer-scale dissipation per useful computation; the supplied report provides no independent full-system audit establishing those broader outcomes.

Herr’s arXiv manuscript models superconducting adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic at 4.2 K. It is internally dated 8 April 2025 and carries an arXiv v1 stamp of 5 April 2025. Under specified fabrication-spread and terminate-gate mismatch assumptions, it estimates dissipation of approximately seven times the Landauer limit in a hypothetical billion-device chip. This is a modeling result in a preprint, rather than a measured chip result. Its discussion includes clock-source and refrigeration accounting, but the approximately sevenfold estimate must not be treated as a demonstrated full-chip wall-plug performance figure or a room-temperature general-purpose processor result.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied materials document a colloidal-bit experiment, preliminary projections, a reported company announcement and superconducting modeling. They do not establish completion of the proposed processor. Because the supplied search record is empty, progress after these sources through 1 November 2026 remains unresolved. That freshness limitation does not invalidate the historical results or show that the unverified APL assertion is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a programmable processor above 273 K on a specified standard integer workload, using the measured operating temperature T in all thermodynamic comparisons. Demonstrate a clock above 1 MHz, average dissipation below 10 kT ln 2 per erased information bit, average dissipation below 10 kT per logically reversible primitive operation, and residual logical error probability below 10⁻¹² per operation after correction. These are proposed milestones from the candidate, not established scientific or industry standards. Above 273 K excludes the cited cryogenic implementation but does not by itself define room temperature; the demonstration should state its actual temperature and intended operating range.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement definitions: specify primitive operations, erased-information counts, workload size, throughput and statistical confidence bounds before testing. Count erased information rather than assuming every physical reset erases one initially unbiased bit. Define how dissipation is allocated between irreversible erasure and reversible operations without double counting. Also report total workload energy divided separately by each operation count, so favorable allocation cannot conceal high system energy.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed measurement definitions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed audit boundary: independently measure total wall-plug energy per completed workload, including the clock or resonator, power conversion, memory, communication and correction. Report recovered internal energy alongside net external consumption, identify any excluded equipment and explain how shared costs are allocated. This audit design addresses the documented possibility that local energy recovery does not translate into reduced external power consumption.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed audit boundary

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: publish enough implementation, workload and measurement information for independent replication. Repeat measurements across representative programs, devices and operating conditions, and report density, sustained throughput, memory requirements and correction overhead. Establish the claimed error probability with stated statistical confidence rather than equating an error-free short run with a 10⁻¹² rate. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth and reliability under tested conditions, not literal universality across all programs or environments.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: THR-08, “Equilibrium sampling computers operating near thermal energy per sample,” is the closest neighboring target. Its supplied title concerns sampling and energy per sample, while THR-03 concerns deterministic programmable digital computation and energy associated with erasure, reversible operations and complete workloads. Both connect computation to thermal energy scales, but their outputs and performance denominators differ. The title alone does not establish that THR-08 is restricted to inference, nor does it provide enough detail to assess its implementation or demonstrated performance.

Roster-based comparison: THR-02, “Useful heat engines that are simultaneously efficient, powerful, and steady,” shares the challenge of combining favorable thermodynamic efficiency with useful operating rate. THR-03 applies that tension to information processing and energy recovery; THR-02 concerns heat-engine performance. THR-05, “A size-extensive quantum advantage in thermodynamic performance,” concerns a quantum advantage, whereas THR-03 does not require quantum computation. The cited superconducting aQFP model supplies a possible low-energy logic approach, not evidence of the size-extensive quantum advantage named by THR-05.

Roster-based comparison: THR-01, “A computable thermodynamic potential for far-from-equilibrium continuum transport,” and THR-11, “Operational temperature and entropy for far-from-equilibrium matter,” address broader thermodynamic descriptions. Their titles suggest methodological connections to understanding driven physical systems, while THR-03 seeks a concrete computing capability. THR-12, “Predictive thermodynamic design of far-from-equilibrium chemical reaction networks,” likewise concerns predictive design, but for chemical networks. These title-level connections do not establish that solving any one is necessary or sufficient to complete THR-03.

Roster-based comparison: THR-04, “Bulk electronic heat–charge decoupling sufficient for engine-class solid-state conversion,” THR-06, “A single-absorber solar converter that uses non-thermal carriers to pass the detailed-balance limit,” and THR-07, “Synthetic chemomechanical engines whose efficiency approaches biological molecular motors,” concern distinct conversion mechanisms and useful outputs. THR-09, “A thermodynamic design theory of self-replicators, confirmed by a predicted non-biological replicator,” targets replication, and THR-10, “A laboratory measurement of the Unruh temperature,” targets a physical measurement. Their supplied titles establish no direct equivalence with low-dissipation programmable computation; each remains a separate innovation.

change_log.change: Qualified the Landauer bound by the initially unbiased classical-bit and isothermal assumptions, and separated erasure evidence from reversible-operation claims.
change_log.reason: The colloidal experiment supports a specific erasure result, not experimental verification of every reversible computation.

change_log.change: Explained logical reversibility, physical energy recovery and workload-level efficiency as distinct requirements.
change_log.reason: Avoiding information erasure does not eliminate switching, control, communication or correction losses.

change_log.change: Retained the 25,200 kT assertion as unverified and distinguished the missing 2025 APL article from the retained 2023 presentation.
change_log.reason: No artifact supports verification of the APL citation or numerical context; the presentation is separate and preliminary.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad numerical CMOS characterization with a qualified qualitative account and preserved roadmap extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The reviewed textual evidence supports scaling constraints but does not establish a universal numerical range or exact floor.

change_log.change: Specified Vaire’s announced tape-out, company attribution and resonator-only energy-recovery denominator.
change_log.reason: The report does not establish independently measured processor operation or full-system Landauer-scale efficiency.

change_log.change: Preserved Herr’s approximate sevenfold estimate while adding its preprint status, two date markers, 4.2 K temperature, hypothetical scale and mismatch assumptions.
change_log.reason: The estimate is modeling evidence, not demonstrated room-temperature or wall-plug processor performance.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria with information counts, operation definitions, energy allocation, workload accounting and error-confidence requirements.
change_log.reason: The original numerical thresholds need explicit denominators and boundaries to be reproducible and meaningful.

change_log.change: Qualified the transistor analogy and added conditional system-level and commercial limits.
change_log.reason: Low energy per erased bit alone does not establish lower energy per useful computation or equivalent economic impact.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster title to explain the limited THR-08 distinction and added title-based relationships to the other entries.
change_log.reason: The roster supports a sampling-versus-digital-computation comparison, but not the original inference-only characterization or detailed technical overlap.

change_log.change: Preserved uncertainty about completion through 1 November 2026.
change_log.reason: An empty freshness search cannot establish either present-day absence or achievement of the complete target.

unresolved_issues: Whether the complete programmable, reliable, near-room-temperature capability had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026 remains unassessed in the supplied evidence.
The 2025 Frank–Edwards APL article’s bibliographic details, 25,200 kT value and numerical context remain unverified because no artifact was retained.
The supplied record does not independently establish operating measurements for Vaire’s announced prototype or the claimed resonator recovery.
Full experimental details of the Nature result and numerical graphical content of the roadmap and preliminary presentation were not established by the supplied review.
The proposed thresholds still require an agreed workload, primitive-operation definition, information-erasure accounting, energy-allocation method and statistical test design.
The proposed above-273 K requirement needs an explicit operating range if room-temperature performance is essential to completion.
Detailed relationships with the roster, particularly THR-08, require definitions and evidence beyond the supplied titles; no inference-only restriction has been retained.

prerequisites.reason: Computation near the Landauer scale is expected to use reversible operations and switching-energy recovery to reduce physical dissipation.
